subject: bat
pitch: A fruit bat with its wings spread wide. A fluffy golden-brown body, a fox-like face with big dark eyes and a moist black nose, pointed ears, and leathery charcoal wings stretched between long finger bones with a small hooked claw on each thumb. It clutches a half-eaten fig in its feet.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module for a flying fruit bat model, wings spread with a fig held in its feet, thinking through pose and scale before writing the code.

Defining joint positions...

Skipping fur cards as risky, I'll instead fake fluffiness by scattering small cone-shaped spikes around the neck and shoulders like a mane, using surface scatter to place around 70 cone geometries with light gold paint oriented outward from the body normal.

Now I'm sketching the head structure: an ellipsoid sphere for the skull, a tapered capsule snout, a small jaw box, a black nose sphere with a tiny highlight, dark eye spheres with white glints, and pointed cone ears with pink inner cones tilted upward.

Working out exact coordinates for the head, snout, nose, and jaw placement, plus adding little fang cones for detail. Now I'm starting on the wing structure, setting up shoulder joints mirrored on each side.

Fanning out the remaining fingers in a natural resting spread, I'll give each one a two-joint chain (metacarpal and phalanx) with a slight curve, parented to the wrist joint for the bend.

Setting up the arm chain similarly, with shoulder, elbow, and wrist as named joints spanning two segments, then attaching the finger chains to the wrist joint reference. Still writing sweep radii...

For the wing membrane, I need membranes connecting adjacent finger chains and the arm chain back to the body, since they all share a root at the wrist — the propatagium connects the arm edge (shoulder to wrist) with the second finger chain (wrist to tip).

Working out the plagiopatagium mapping...

I realize the proper quad is bounded by the arm edge, finger5, the trailing edge from hip to tip5, and the body edge from hip to shoulder, so at t=1 the cross-edge is exactly wrist→tip5, confirming this forms the correct boundary.

For weights, the arm chain governs the A side while B falls back to the other chain's joints along the trailing path, giving a smooth mixed blend that's fine in rest pose even though the hip point would otherwise move with the arm. I can set a bone option on path edges to make them rigid to a specific joint (like root) while chain edges follow their own bone, which handles the rigidity nicely. For the middle finger quads (M2-M4 between adjacent fingers), both sides A and B are just the respective finger chains, which is simpler.

I'm now adding a propatagium membrane — the leading edge membrane bats have running from the shoulder forward to the thumb — defined as a polyline from near the neck forward to the thumb tip, offset slightly ahead of the arm chain to form a thin forward strip. I'm setting membrane thickness and giving it a mottled charcoal paint shared across all the membrane meshes, then double-checking the winding/normals so the closed prism geometry renders correctly on both sides.

Now I'm working out the finger joint and tip coordinates for each wing finger (f2 through f5), placing them at varying forward/backward and up/down positions to shape the wing's silhouette, aiming for a roughly 1.85 wingspan once mirrored across both sides.

The trailing edge connects to tip5, and I'll trace the hind leg membrane path from the hip point to that fifth finger tip. I'll skip the small uropatagium between the legs for now and decide whether to add a tail separately.

Fruit bats don't have tails, so I'll skip that entirely. For the thumb, I'm setting up a short capsule chain from the wrist to the thumb tip with a hooked claw spike at the end.

Writing thumb geometry...

Now I'm mirroring the whole setup across sides, treating +X as the left side, and working out the leg placement: hips attach near the belly, with knees and ankles hanging down to grasp the fig positioned below the body at roughly its center.

Sizing the fig relative to the fruit bat's body so it sits with its bottom at ground level, then placing feet at the fig's top surface and working out hip-knee-ankle chains that bend backward like a bat's leg, with toes wrapping over the fig's curved top.

Working out the toe wrapping math...

Still computing toe positions...

Still working out joint placement...

Checking the ankle-to-toe distance looks reasonable for the leg chains. For the fig, I'm planning a lathe-based teardrop shape held in the feet, oriented with the stem pointing backward and the bitten end facing toward the bat's mouth.

Still writing the lathe profile...

Adjusting the lathe coordinates...

Still defining dish outlines...

Now I'm thinking about adding scattered seed details on the dish surface, using small spheres placed via surface scattering filtered by normal direction so they sit naturally on the flesh.

I also want the flesh coloring to have a radial gradient from pale pith at the edges to deep red near the center, implemented as a custom paint function based on distance from the axis, plus a mottled purple skin texture.

For the fig's placement I'm working out the lathe orientation along the z-axis and nudging its center height so the bottom barely touches the floor without clipping through it, adjusting the radius and segment count accordingly.

I need a bone for the fig, so I'm creating a dedicated "fig" joint parented to root at the fig's center rather than trying to attach it to an existing toe joint, then explicitly assigning that bone to the fig part. Now I'm setting up the body's loft stations along z with width/height cross-sections and y-centers at each slice to build the main silhouette.

Working through the frame math, I confirm that with tangent pointing +Z, the sweep's normal axis aligns with world up and binormal with side, so ry controls height and rx controls width as intended. I'm placing the chest and belly stations, then setting the hip joint position relative to the body width at that z-slice.

For coloring, I'll use a countershade paint combining mottled textures for back and belly tones, nesting the mottle noise inside the countershade so the gradient transitions naturally with some softness. The fluffy tuft cones can just use simple solid colors since the countershade effect depends on surface normals, and I'll keep the stick geometry parts lightweight even with 70+ pieces.

Now I'm planning the neck ruff and mantle as scattered tufts filtered by z-position on the body surface, using a golden lighter color for the shoulder collar and a slightly different shade for the chest mantle, with counts around 40-100 tufts each. I need to make sure the body surface is fully built before scattering since the tufts are separate parts, not part of the surface mesh itself, and the body mesh needs proper skin weights blended across the spine joint chain for correct deformation.

For the loft, I'm confirming that passing the spine chain as the bone source works correctly since it uses its own joints, and the loft path can reference the chain's owner directly with default rounded caps. Then I'm working out the head geometry: a scaled ellipsoid sphere positioned on the head joint, with a lighter tan muzzle and darker forehead coloring, plus eye spheres with calculated glint positions offset along a normalized direction vector from the eye center.

I'm checking that the eye spheres sit properly relative to the head ellipsoid surface using a normalized point test, confirming they protrude slightly as intended. Then I'm defining the snout as a tapering tube swept from the head toward the nose tip with shrinking radii for a fox-like taper, topped with a small black nose sphere, a tiny white highlight, and starting to plan the nostril details.

Now I'm adding the lower jaw as a tapering capsule swept from the jaw joint forward, plus small cone-shaped teeth placed on both upper and lower jaw, accepting that the closed mouth will mostly hide them. I'm settling on a neutral closed-mouth pose and moving on to building the ears as tall tilted cones angled outward from the head.

Still defining ear geometry...

I'm scattering small fur tufts across the back of the head using a surface distribution, filtering to keep the front face smooth. Skipping brow and whisker details, and planning to move on to fur sweeps along the upper arms.

For the arms, I'm setting up a tapered sweep with gold-brown color near the shoulder transitioning to charcoal at the forearm, using color bands to cut the mesh accordingly. Then for claws, I'm giving thumb claws a pale ivory tone and tapering small cone-like sweeps at the toe tips for foot claws.

For legs, I'm building hip-to-knee-to-ankle chains with tapered fur-colored sweeps, then attaching toe chains at the ankle joint, making sure to pick joint naming conventions (like toe1L1) that avoid ambiguous overlaps with default naming patterns.

I need to explicitly set chain parents since the default parent inference won't work correctly here: legs should attach to spine1, arms to spine2, and toe chains to their respective ankle joints. I'm also checking that polyline knot counts translate correctly to spans and joint names for legs, arms, fingers, and toes, and assigning role types like "arm" and "digit" for the various chains.

For membranes, I'm defining them as edges between finger chains with a scallop parameter that curves the trailing edge concave by pulling the midpoint back toward the base—around 0.12 seems right, with row count bumped up to 5 for smoother detail.

Now I'm working out the fan ordering of finger membranes (f2–f5) around the wrist based on their angular tip positions, and setting up a quad membrane connecting the arm chain to the hip-to-f5-tip path so the wrist-to-finger5 edge aligns properly without overlapping the region already covered by the f4-f5 membrane.

For skinning, I'm defining bone-weighted edges for path vertices so each owner joint drives its own chain, defaulting to root rigidity where needed. For the membrane surface paint, I'm combining a mottled charcoal texture with a subtle purple-brown tint rather than adding extra vein detail, then baking that paint onto each membrane mesh and mirroring the whole setup across left and right sides in a loop.

I'm estimating total part counts (tufts roughly 124) and triangle counts for the membranes, confirming the geometry stays lightweight even across five mirrored membrane panels. Then I start writing the actual build script, setting up the builder and root joint definition.

Still writing skeleton joints... spine chain, neck, head, and jaw are all being positioned and parented in sequence.

Then I'm checking the gap between the body loft end and head sphere, adding a neck capsule to bridge them, and setting up surface scattering helpers for adding tufts via cone geometry sampled across the body mesh.

Computing lean direction for frame...

Thinking about shared geometry reuse across parts versus cloning for blended meshes, and filtering collar tufts by z-position for a bigger cone shape.

Now I'm setting up the head geometry as a scaled unit sphere with mottled brown paint tones, checking that non-uniform scaling still transforms normals correctly through the normal matrix for proper shading.

Then I move to building the wing skeleton: looping over left/right sides to create mirrored arm chains with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints as polylines, then defining finger chains parented to each wrist with their own point paths.

Writing finger sweeps...

For the thumb I'm setting up a shorter chain with its own radius taper and darker color, then adding a curved claw sweep from the fingertip using control points angled forward and down for a hooked shape.

Still defining membrane geometry...

Now I'm moving on to the leg chain, laying out the hip-to-ankle polyline points to shape the leg skeleton.

Still working out leg geometry...

Still defining claw placement and bone attachment...

Now I'm thinking through the fig's shape and orientation—it's lathed along the z-axis with a profile radius maxing around .062, so the fig extends from roughly c.z-.075 to c.z+.056. I'm figuring out where to place the bite mark at the +z end.

The toes are positioned at a larger radius than the fig's surface at those z-offsets, so they'd float above the skin instead of touching it—I need to adjust the toe z-offsets so they actually contact the fig's surface at the correct radius.

Defining toe placement using angle offsets and a radius interpolation function over the profile array, checking that the lowest point of the lathe-generated shape lands near y=0.0005 so the base sits flat.

Adding figure stem geometry and skin paint logic...

Scattering seed speckles onto the flesh dish while making sure the buried-point test only checks against the flesh mesh itself, since it's a closed lathe shape. I'm adding a fig stem joint parented to root, and considering a darker ring sphere behind the eyes for depth, skipping brows for now.

Settling on placing a small darkened mask sphere just behind each eye center and the eye sphere slightly in front of it, then double-checking the typing so point tuples and number arrays are accepted by the part placement function. Writing the fur gradient function call with gold tones and countershading before continuing into body placement...

Defining the body loft with graduated widths bound to the spine, verifying bottom dimensions line up against the hip position, and setting up vertex weight scatter for tufts. Now I'm working out the ear joint placement with a direction vector from the head, preparing to build the outer ear cone geometry...

Writing cone geometry params...

Finishing up the inner ear cone offset forward from the outer one, then moving to the head ruff scatter filtered by z-position, and defining the snout's tapering radius function for the sweep geometry before returning the final root.

Now I'm adding the lower jaw as a capsule bone, placing upper and lower fang teeth as tiny rotated cones attached to the head and jaw bones respectively, and building the neck as a colored capsule sweep connecting to the body.

For the chain joints, I'm verifying the names array matches the span count, then writing the leg sweeps with tapered radii and a brownish tint tied to each leg's own joint chain, followed by the finger sweeps using the same colored chain approach.
